title: What caused the cocoliztli epidemics of 1545 and 1576 in New Spain?
short: Two epidemics that Nahua and Spanish observers called cocoliztli killed a large share of central Mexico's Indigenous population, and their cause, whether a native haemorrhagic fever, enteric fever or something else, is disputed.

needs.ask: Screen securely dated 1545 and 1576 epidemic burials beyond Teposcolula-Yucundaa with methods able to recover RNA viruses and parasites as well as bacteria.
State what the drought-and-rodent, colonial-disruption and contagion-along-routes models predict for the timing, geography and victims of mortality, and test them against the documentary atlas.
Compare the Stahle gridded soil-moisture reconstructions with dated, georeferenced epidemic reports for 1545 and 1576, and state where drought preceded mortality.

matters: The cocoliztli epidemics of 1545–48 and 1576–80 are counted among the largest mortality events in the sixteenth-century collapse of Mexico's Indigenous population, with contemporary and modern estimates of losses ranging widely and in some accounts exceeding the toll of the 1520 smallpox epidemic. Whether they were caused by a pathogen introduced from Europe or Africa, by a native disease released by drought and colonial disruption, or by several agents together changes how the collapse is explained: as an inevitable consequence of contact, or as the product of colonial labour, resettlement and famine acting on susceptible populations.
stuck: The clinical descriptions (high fever, bleeding from nose and mouth, jaundice, rapid death, Indigenous victims and few Spanish ones) fit several modern diseases, and sixteenth-century terms like cocoliztli ('pestilence') were generic. Rodolfo Acuña-Soto and colleagues proposed a native rodent-borne haemorrhagic fever amplified by drought, but no such virus has been identified, and RNA viruses rarely survive to be detected in skeletal remains. Vågene et al. (2018) recovered Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C from an epidemic cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, but from one site in the Mixteca Alta and with the acknowledged possibility that other, undetectable pathogens were also present, so the finding has not settled the question for 1545 in central Mexico or for 1576 at all.
solved: Pathogen evidence from several independently dated epidemic burials of 1545–48 and 1576–80, in central Mexico as well as Oaxaca, identifies the same agent or combination of agents, and the agent's known epidemiology is consistent with the timing, symptoms, age and ethnic pattern of mortality, and geography recorded in the Relaciones geográficas, parish and cabildo records.
approach: Build on the demographic and documentary work of Cook (1991), McCaa (1995) and Cook (1998), the haemorrhagic-fever case made by Acuña-Soto (2000) and Marr (2000), and the drought argument of Acuña-Soto (2002). The pictorial annals, read through Mengin (1952), and recent readings of the Florentine Codex by Ríos Castaño (2025) show how much the Nahuatl sources still have to give.

Extract every report of the 1545 and 1576 epidemics from the Relaciones geográficas of 1579–85, Sahagún's writings, Francisco Hernández, Juan de Torquemada, the Codex en Cruz and Codex Mexicanus, viceregal correspondence and the Mexico City cabildo minutes. Each report becomes a record of symptoms, dates, place, mortality claim and who died, with Spanish and Nahuatl testimony kept distinct and the date of writing recorded, since many accounts were set down decades after the events.

A georeferenced, source-graded atlas of the two epidemics would be useful on its own terms, showing where the documentary record is dense, where it is silent, and how far later chroniclers copied one another.

Set the atlas against the gridded soil-moisture reconstructions of Stahle (2016) and against the spread of cattle, wheat, congregación and repartimiento labour. A drought-and-rodent reservoir model, a colonial-disruption model and a contagion-along-routes model predict different geographies and timings of mortality, and the comparison should be reviewed by historians of New Spain before any is preferred.

Treat the pathogen as an open question. The Salmonella Paratyphi C genomes from Teposcolula-Yucundaa reported by Vågene (2018), with the context in Warinner (2012), Zhou (2018) and Bravo-Lopez (2025), establish one infection at one site, not the cause of the whole epidemic; mortality totals, too, will stay a wide range.

Testing that result depends on INAH and palaeogenomic laboratories: identifying securely dated epidemic burials in Mexico City, Puebla, Oaxaca and elsewhere, and screening them with methods able to recover RNA viruses and parasites as well as bacteria, under protocols agreed with descendant communities.

existing.title: Commentaire du Codex Mexicanus nos 23-24 de la Bibliothèque Nationale de Paris
existing.venue: Journal de la Société des Américanistes 41 (2): 387–498
existing.note: Standard commentary on the Codex Mexicanus, whose annals record epidemic years in pictorial form.

existing.authors: Noble David Cook and W. George Lovell (eds.)
existing.title: "Secret Judgments of God": Old World Disease in Colonial Spanish America
existing.note: Collected essays on epidemics in Spanish America, including Hanns Prem's chronology of disease outbreaks in sixteenth-century central Mexico.

existing.title: Spanish and Nahuatl Views on Smallpox and Demographic Catastrophe in Mexico
existing.note: Compared Spanish and Nahuatl sources on the sixteenth-century epidemics and the weight they assign to smallpox relative to later outbreaks.

existing.title: Born to Die: Disease and New World Conquest, 1492–1650
existing.note: Synthesis of epidemic disease in the conquest of the Americas that places the 1545 and 1576 epidemics within a sequence of Old World introductions.

existing.authors: Rodolfo Acuña-Soto, L. Calderón Romero and James H. Maguire
existing.title: Large epidemics of hemorrhagic fevers in Mexico 1545–1815
existing.venue: American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene 62 (6): 733–739
existing.note: Argued that the 1545 and 1576 epidemics and later colonial outbreaks were a haemorrhagic fever of unknown, probably native, origin, and that the 1576 epidemic killed about 45 percent of the population.

existing.authors: John S. Marr and James B. Kiracofe
existing.title: Was the Huey Cocoliztli a haemorrhagic fever?
existing.note: Reviewed the clinical descriptions of the 1576 epidemic, including Francisco Hernández's, against candidate diagnoses and assessed the haemorrhagic fever hypothesis.

existing.authors: Rodolfo Acuña-Soto, David W. Stahle, Malcolm K. Cleaveland and Matthew D. Therrell
existing.title: Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico
existing.note: Used a Douglas-fir tree-ring reconstruction to show that both epidemics coincided with severe drought, proposing that wet years after drought amplified rodent hosts of a native virus.

existing.authors: Rodolfo Acuña-Soto, David W. Stahle, Matthew D. Therrell, Richard D. Griffin and Malcolm K. Cleaveland
existing.title: When half of the population died: the epidemic of hemorrhagic fevers of 1576 in Mexico
existing.note: Restated the case for a native haemorrhagic fever in 1576 using contemporary descriptions and the drought record.

existing.authors: Christina Warinner, Nelly Robles García, Ronald Spores and Noreen Tuross
existing.title: Disease, Demography, and Diet in Early Colonial New Spain: Investigation of a Sixteenth-Century Mixtec Cemetery at Teposcolula Yucundaa
existing.note: Identified the Teposcolula Yucundaa burials as the earliest known colonial epidemic cemetery in Mexico, linked to the cocoliztli of 1544–50, and showed the dead were local Mixtecs.

existing.authors: David W. Stahle, Edward R. Cook, Dorian J. Burnette, José Villanueva, Julián Cerano et al.
existing.title: The Mexican Drought Atlas: Tree-ring reconstructions of the soil moisture balance during the late pre-Hispanic, colonial, and modern eras
existing.note: Gridded summer soil-moisture reconstructions for Mexico from 1400 CE, built from 252 tree-ring chronologies, allowing drought to be mapped year by year against epidemic reports.

existing.authors: Åshild J. Vågene, Alexander Herbig, Michael G. Campana, Nelly M. Robles García, Christina Warinner, Susanna Sabin et al.
existing.title: Salmonella enterica genomes from victims of a major sixteenth-century epidemic in Mexico
existing.note: Metagenomic screening of Teposcolula Yucundaa burials recovered Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C genomes, proposed as a strong candidate for the 1545 epidemic while not excluding other pathogens.

existing.authors: Zhemin Zhou, Inge Lundstrøm, Alicia Tran-Dien, Sebastián Duchêne, Nabil-Fareed Alikhan, Martin J. Sergeant et al.
existing.title: Pan-genome Analysis of Ancient and Modern Salmonella enterica Demonstrates Genomic Stability of the Invasive Para C Lineage for Millennia
existing.note: A Paratyphi C genome from a c. 1200 CE Norwegian burial showed the lineage was present in medieval Europe, consistent with but not proof of a European introduction to Mexico.

existing.authors: Oscar René Benavides Cárabes and Carlos Viesca Treviño
existing.title: Changes in indigenous dress and the cocoliztli epidemic of 1544–1548 in New Spain
existing.note: Proposed that colonial changes in Indigenous clothing and living conditions favoured louse-borne transmission, reviving a typhus-related interpretation.

existing.title: Religion over Life and Death. The Cocoliztli in the Florentine Codex
existing.venue: In R. Radlwimmer (ed.), Bodies, Remedies, Policies. Berlin: De Gruyter: 69–88
existing.note: Study of how Sahagún's Florentine Codex, compiled in the years of the 1576 epidemic, presents the cocoliztli and frames its meaning.

existing.authors: Miriam Bravo-Lopez, Eduardo Arrieta-Donato, Viridiana Villa-Islas, Åshild J. Vågene et al. and María C. Ávila-Arcos
existing.title: Ancient genomic insights into Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C from Central Mexico
existing.note: A nineteenth-century Paratyphi C genome from Mexico City clustered with the Teposcolula genomes, with divergence estimates the authors read as a colonial-era European introduction followed by local persistence (not yet peer reviewed).

archives.repository: Benson Latin American Collection, University of Texas at Austin
archives.collection: Relaciones Geográficas of Mexico and Guatemala (1577–1585), with painted maps
archives.note: Responses to the crown questionnaire, many of which report population loss and the 1576 epidemic town by town; digitized and openly accessible.

holdings.name: Relaciones Geográficas of Mexico and Guatemala, Joaquín García Icazbalceta Manuscript Collection
holdings.note: Forty-three responses to the 1577 questionnaire, several of which report the epidemics and population loss; transcriptions are in progress on FromThePage.

holdings.name: Relación geográfica map of Cholula (1581)
holdings.note: One of the painted maps from the same collection, catalogued item by item at the Library of Congress as part of the World Digital Library.

archives.collection: Relaciones geográficas held in Spain, Audiencia de México correspondence of viceroys and officials, and Mapas y Planos
archives.note: Viceregal and ecclesiastical reports on the epidemics, tribute losses and remedies, searchable and partly imaged through PARES.

holdings.name: Audiencia de México
holdings.note: Correspondence of viceroys, audiencia and officials with the Council of the Indies, the main Spanish-side source for reports on epidemics, tribute losses and remedies.

archives.collection: Florentine Codex (Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España), Med. Palat. 218–220
archives.note: Sahagún's bilingual Nahuatl and Spanish encyclopedia, compiled with Nahua collaborators during the 1576 epidemic and including comments on it; fully digitized in the Getty's Digital Florentine Codex.

holdings.name: Florentine Codex (Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España)
holdings.note: Sahagún's twelve-book Nahuatl and Spanish encyclopedia, compiled with Nahua collaborators; the Getty edition gives the Laurenziana manuscript in full with transcription.

holdings.name: Florentine Codex, Book XII: The Conquest of Mexico
holdings.note: Nahua account of the 1520 smallpox epidemic, the baseline against which later epidemics were compared; World Digital Library scan at the Library of Congress.

archives.collection: Manuscrits mexicains, including the Codex Mexicanus (Mexicain 23–24) and the Codex en Cruz
archives.note: Nahua annals that record the epidemic years in pictorial form, including a 1545 image of a figure bleeding from nose and mouth in the Codex Mexicanus.

holdings.name: Codex Mexicanus
holdings.note: Pictorial Nahua annals on amate bark paper (51 leaves) that record the 1545 epidemic; Mengin (1952) is the standard study.

archives.repository: Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico City
archives.collection: Ramos Indios, Mercedes, General de Parte and Hospital de Jesús; parish and tribute records
archives.note: Viceregal orders on tribute relief, hospitals and labour during the epidemics, and local petitions describing deaths.

holdings.name: Fondo Hospital de Jesús
holdings.note: Papers of the Hospital de Jesús, 1520 to 1925, relevant to Indigenous labour, estates and hospital provision in the sixteenth century.

archives.repository: Archivo Histórico de la Ciudad de México
archives.collection: Actas de Cabildo del Ayuntamiento de México (published 1889 onward)
archives.note: Minutes of the Mexico City council recording food supply, burials and public health measures in the epidemic years; nineteenth-century printed volumes are online.

holdings.name: Actas de Cabildo del Ayuntamiento de la Ciudad de México (printed edition)
holdings.note: Nineteenth-century printed transcription of the sixteenth-century council minutes, with scanned volumes on the Internet Archive; the volumes covering 1545-48 and 1576-80 should be identified from the printed indexes.

archives.repository: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH), Oaxaca and Mexico City
archives.collection: Skeletal collections from the Teposcolula Yucundaa epidemic cemetery and other colonial burial assemblages
archives.note: The human remains on which any pathogen identification depends; sampling requires INAH permits and collaboration with Mexican researchers.
